_keylessComment: The allow list holds the verbs that only REPORT. None of them runs a command
the caller chose and none can print a value, so a prompt on them asks a person
to approve a listing. Unapproved, an agent stops to ask before it can even
find out which names exist — and the next thing it reaches for is the file
the deny list below exists to keep it out of.
`keyless run` is DELIBERATELY ABSENT, and this is the entry people will want
to add. `Bash(keyless run:*)` matches every command anyone can put after the
`--`, so it does not approve `keyless`; it approves arbitrary execution with
`keyless run` as the prefix. The prompt on a `run` is the prompt for the
command being run, and that one is correct. Adding it to your own settings is
your call to make; shipping it to everybody is not this pack's.
`new` and `put` are absent for the other reason: they WRITE to a store.
The deny list below holds only OPAQUE credential stores — files whose names
are worthless to an agent and whose content is never legitimately needed.
For those a hard permission gate is strictly better than the hook: it
survives a broken hook, bypassPermissions, and the subagent boundary.
`.env` and friends are deliberately ABSENT, and that is a measured decision.
A permission deny PRE-EMPTS the hook's rewrite. Driven live: with
Read(**/.env) in this list the session was told only 'denied by permission
settings' — no names, no alternative. With it removed, the same session was
told which three names the file declares and offered
`keyless run -s <NAME> -- <cmd>`. The hook is the better layer for a file
worth inventorying; the deny rule is the better layer for a file that is
nothing but key material.
`_keylessHardDeny` adds the wider list for anyone who wants the hard gate
anyway: `./install.sh --hard-deny`. It costs the names view.
install.py copies `hooks` and `permissions.deny` into your settings file and
nothing else. Neither comment key is ever written there.
